name: Nora Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a cell of three five-axis CNC machines at a precision shop that makes medical implants, mostly titanium hip stems and knee parts. A five-axis machine is a cutter that can come at the metal from almost any angle, so you can carve really complex shapes in one go. My day is loading blanks, checking the first part off each batch on the measuring machine, and tweaking programs when the tolerance drifts. The parts go inside people, so we measure to a few thousandths of a millimetre, and I love that it matters that much.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned tweaking programs. Do you use any AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I paste in a chunk of machine code and ask a chatbot why the tool path is chattering on one corner, and it's right more often than you'd think. My supervisor Hugo was suspicious at first, but now he sends me the weird problems. At home I use it for everything, from meal plans to arguing with my landlord about the boiler, which I won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that it's a really good tool and people expected it to be a god. On my socials I'd post a little thread on what actually worked in our shop and what didn't. I'd probably get into an argument with someone who thinks it's all a scam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointed. I like my job, but I'd been hoping AI would let me move up into programming the machines rather than babysitting them. In this picture I'd still get there, just the slow way, by doing the night course and waiting for Hugo to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I use now and push to get the shop's programming software upgraded so I can do more of the setup myself. I'd sign up for the CAM programming course, that's computer-aided machining, where you design the cutting paths on screen, and pay for it out of savings. Otherwise, carry on, keep saving, and keep moaning about the boiler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly bored. Like a film that was hyped and was just fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting for Hugo to retire. Is there tension there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, he's lovely, he brings his wife's lemon cake on Fridays. But there's only one programmer job in a shop our size, and he's 61. In the boring version of the future, my career plan is basically lemon cake and patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about a plateau that you'd be glad of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my friends who work in offices wouldn't be panicking. My flatmate Leila writes adverts and she's been doom-scrolling about AI for a year. If it plateaued, she'd sleep better, and so would I, because she'd stop waking me up to talk about it.

S0.say: I'd say it's a really good tool that people expected to be a god. I'd post a thread about what worked in our shop and argue with anyone calling it a scam.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped AI would speed my move into programming. I'd still get there, just slowly.
S0.do: Keeps using her current tools and pushes for upgraded programming software at the shop. Signs up for a CAM programming course paid from savings and otherwise carries on.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, like a hyped film that turned out fine.
S0.quote: In the boring version of the future, my career plan is basically lemon cake and patience.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is the rare operator who wants faster change, because she sees AI as her ladder into programming. A plateau mostly costs her time. She is warm about her supervisor Hugo even while waiting for his job, and finds relief in the plateau mainly on behalf of anxious friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we should want, real change with time to adjust. I'd push online for proper public training funds, because not everyone has my savings or my nerdy streak. At work I'd volunteer to be the person who trials the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd come out of it well. Our shop would bring in automatic loading and AI-written tool paths, and someone has to make them work on real titanium with real tolerances. That's me, if I move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month one, I'd go to Hugo and the owner with a plan to put a robot loader on my cell, because then one person runs six machines instead of three. I'd do the CAM course and get certified on the robot brand they choose. I'd use part of my savings for the course and a decent laptop, around two thousand all in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest. Then guilty for being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because one person running six machines means somebody else isn't running three. That somebody is probably Rui on nights, who's only been here two years. I'd be the one designing the change that makes Rui's job vanish, and I'd want to be the one who helps him land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help him land, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach him the measuring machine, because inspection is the bit the robots are worst at. I'd push for the shop to keep him on through training, and I'd back the union on that, even though our shop is barely unionised. I can do both, be keen on the robots and still be on the workers' side.

S1.say: I'd say this is the version we should want, real change with time to adjust. I'd push for public training funds and volunteer to trial new systems at work.
S1.think: Privately I'd come out of it well, because someone has to make AI tool paths and robot loading work on real titanium. That's me, if I move fast.
S1.do: Pitches a robot loader for her cell in the first month so one person runs six machines. Takes the CAM course, gets certified on the chosen robot and spends about two thousand of her savings on training and a laptop.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, followed by guilt about the excitement.
S1.quote: I'd be the one designing the change that makes Rui's job vanish, and I'd want to be the one who helps him land.
S1.fieldNote: Nora would be an active driver of automation and is honest that it cuts others' jobs. Her guilt about Rui is real, and she answers it with concrete steps like teaching him inspection. She refuses to see being pro-robot and pro-worker as a contradiction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and public ownership of some of this stuff, and I'd mean it. I'd be loud about it online, sharing plans that have actually been costed. At work I'd tell people not to panic and to get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my adaptability doesn't save me here. Being early to the tools only helps if there's a gap between people who learn them and the machines that replace them, and two years closes that gap. I'd be fine for money for a while, but I'd be one of millions with nothing to adapt to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job as long as it lasted and spend the first year helping the shop automate safely, because those parts go inside people and somebody has to check them. I'd move most of my savings into a mix of cash and a broad index fund, since if robots do the work, owning a sliver of the companies is the only share I'd get. And I'd join a political campaign for a basic income, properly, door knocking, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own rent so much as for everyone around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own a sliver of the companies. Doesn't that sit awkwardly with public ownership?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely, and I know it. I'd vote and campaign for the public to own the robots, and in the meantime I'd make sure I'm not the only one at the table with nothing. I'll argue for the fair version all day, but I won't stand in the rain on principle while it's being decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She cleans offices and she's 58, she doesn't have savings like mine. If cleaning robots arrive in two years she'd fall straight through. I'd probably have her move in with Leila and me, and Leila would have to be fine with that.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and public ownership of some of this, and I'd say it loudly. I'd share costed plans and tell people at work to organise rather than panic.
S2.think: Privately my adaptability doesn't save me, because two years closes the gap between learning tools and being replaced. I'd be fine for money for a while, but one of millions with nothing to adapt to.
S2.do: Stays in her job and helps the shop automate safely in the first year. Moves most savings into cash and a broad index fund, campaigns door to door for a basic income and plans for her mother to move in.
S2.feel: Anxious, less for her own rent than for everyone around her.
S2.quote: I'll argue for the fair version all day, but I won't stand in the rain on principle while it's being decided.
S2.fieldNote: Her early adopter advantage disappears, and she knows exactly why. She admits the tension between campaigning for public ownership and buying index funds herself. Her deepest worry is her mother, a 58-year-old cleaner with no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to decide who owns the robots, and that's the only question that matters. I'd be pushing hard for a basic income trial and for workers to get shares in the firms that automate. At work I'd want our shop to automate with its people, not around them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a sweet spot for me. I could ride the wave for three or four years, programming and installing the machines that replace the old way, and build up money. I'd still hit the same wall, but I'd hit it with more savings and more options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the CAM course in the first year and then try to move into an automation engineer role, maybe at the robot supplier itself, which pays more. I'd put a slice of each pay rise into the index fund. I'd also volunteer for the basic income campaign a couple of evenings a month, and start teaching Mum to use the AI tools so she has more choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a wall at the end, but I can see a road up to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would teaching your mum look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday afternoons with her phone and a lot of patience. She already uses voice messages, so I'd start with asking it things out loud. If my mum can get a chatbot to write her a CV, nobody gets to say they're too old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wall is still there. What do you picture on the other side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe a shorter week and a basic income and people making things for the fun of it. Or maybe a few people owning everything and the rest of us renting from them, which is why I'd be in that campaign.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to decide who owns the robots, and that's the only question. I'd push for a basic income trial, worker shares in automating firms, and automation with people rather than around them.
S3.think: Privately five years is a sweet spot, because I could ride the wave for a few years and build savings. I'd hit the same wall with more money and more options.
S3.do: Takes the CAM course in year one, then aims for an automation engineer job, possibly at the robot supplier. Puts part of each pay rise into an index fund, volunteers for the basic income campaign and teaches her mother AI tools on Sundays.
S3.feel: Uneasy, seeing a wall at the end but a clear road up to it.
S3.quote: If my mum can get a chatbot to write her a CV, nobody gets to say they're too old.
S3.fieldNote: Five years plays to her strengths: enough time to profit from the transition before it ends. She keeps a hopeful and a grim version of the outcome in mind and picks political action as the hinge. Teaching her mother is both practical and a quiet act of protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a fair system before it arrives, and if we don't, that's a choice. I'd want the government to start a basic income pilot now and expand it. Online I'd keep it practical, sharing courses and pilots, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Ten years is a whole career in automation for someone who loves this stuff. By 2036 I'd be 37, hopefully a senior engineer with savings, and I'd hope the politics had caught up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, CAM course and robot certification, then a move into automation engineering within two or three years. I'd keep investing every month and maybe buy a flat with my partner, if I've got one by then, Leila keeps saying that's my real project. Later in the decade I'd look at something that mixes engineering with policy, like advising unions on automation deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly hopeful. A small worry that ten years makes everyone lazy about planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why lazy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people think ten years is forever. I watched my old classmates say climate change was for later. Ten years is long enough for everyone to put it off for nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if the ten years got wasted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments first, because they're the only ones who can redistribute at that scale. Then the companies, for lobbying against every tax. But also people like me, who see it coming and keep quiet because we're doing fine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to build a fair system first, so failing would be a choice. I'd want a basic income pilot started now and keep my posts practical rather than gloomy.
S4.think: Privately I'd expect to do well, with a full career in automation ahead of me. By 37 I'd hope to be a senior engineer with savings, and for the politics to have caught up.
S4.do: Completes the CAM course and robot certification in year one and moves into automation engineering within two or three years. Invests monthly, considers buying a flat, and later looks at advising unions on automation deals.
S4.feel: Calm and mostly hopeful, with a small worry that the long timeline makes everyone lazy.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for everyone to put it off for nine.
S4.fieldNote: Nora sees ten years as a career runway for herself and a test for society. She worries that a long horizon breeds delay and compares it to climate change. She includes comfortable people like herself among those who would be to blame.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because being quick doesn't help when everyone falls at once, and people like my mum would fall hardest. I'm good at change, but I can't out-learn a machine that learns faster than everyone. What would help is a basic income that starts before the layoffs, not after, and a public stake in the companies that own the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd actually miss. It's the first-off part, when you measure the first hip stem of a batch and it's perfect to the thousandth. A robot can do that too, but I'd miss being the one.

headlineQuote: I'm good at change, but I can't out-learn a machine that learns faster than everyone.
portrait: Nora Silva, 27, runs a cell of five-axis CNC machines making titanium implants and uses AI tools every day, both at work and at home. She is eager for faster change, which she sees as her way into programming and automation engineering, while staying firmly on the side of workers and public ownership. She stays calm through a plateau and steady disruption, even pitching a robot loader for her own cell and feeling guilty about a junior colleague. Fast AGI makes her anxious, mostly for her mother, a cleaner with no savings. Five and ten years become a runway for her career and a test of whether politics can keep up.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because adaptability can't help when everyone falls at once, and people like her mother would fall hardest.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that starts before the layoffs rather than after, and a public stake in the companies that own the robots.
